bib.title: Routine: A Structural Planning Framework for LLM Agent System in Enterprise

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Routine: A Structural Planning Framework for LLM Agent System in Enterprise", Zeng, Chen, Hu, Qi et al. (Digital China AI Research), arXiv 2507.14447v2, 22 Jul 2025. Preprint, "Under review". File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/03-agentic-foundations/sources/zeng-2025-routine.pdf

COVERAGE: 85,735 chars total. Read 0-60,850 (body, ablations, limits, conclusion) and 72,700-85,735 (Appendices A and B, all prompts). Skipped about 60,850-72,700 (reference list, only its first entries seen) because it is bibliography. Extraction was clean.

FIT WARNING: Partial fit. The paper compares "no plan" vs "expert-written plan" for step-level tool-call accuracy. It does NOT compare against ReAct, or plan-then-act with a model-generated plan on a task benchmark. It measures no cost, latency or token counts. The "No Routine" baseline is a single-turn prompt (user query plus tool list) with no ReAct scaffold. It is one internal HR scenario with synthetic, GPT-4o-distilled test data. Use it as evidence that a precise plan naming the tool per step fixes tool selection, not as a ReAct vs planning result.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. An explicit routine (plan) lifts overall tool-call accuracy a lot, mostly by fixing tool selection.
 number: GPT-4o 41.1 -> 96.3 (branch routine; 97.0 without branches); Qwen3-14B 32.6 -> 83.3; GPT-4-Turbo 43.5 -> 99.0; Claude-3.7-Sonnet 43.9 -> 99.3; Qwen2.5-7B 14.9 -> 49.7
 setup: HR agent, 25 MCP tools, 7 routines (4-7 steps each). 1,148 step-level test samples decomposed from 200 distilled traces. Overall accuracy requires structure, tool and parameters all correct. Single run, no variance reported.
 quote: "GPT-4o achieved an overall accuracy of 96.3% on the scenario-specific test set with Routine planning, significantly outperforming its accuracy of 41.1% without Routine. Similarly, Qwen3-14B's performance improved from 32.6% to 83.3%"
 where: Introduction, p.2; Table 2, p.14
2. Without a routine, tool selection is the dominant failure.
 number: over 85% of errors; no baseline model above 50% overall
 setup: same as above; models GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, Qwen3-8B/14B. Structural accuracy is 94-100% and parameter accuracy 95-98% even with no routine (Table 2).
 quote: "Without Routine guidance, all baseline models performed poorly, with none exceeding 50% overall accuracy... Tool selection errors were identified as the main cause of failure, accounting for over 85% of all errors."
 where: 5.2.1, pp.13-14
3. Naming the tool in each step is the key ingredient. Removing the tool names drops accuracy 5-15 points for most models.
 number: Qwen3-14B 83.3 -> 71.9; Qwen2.5-14B 79.1 -> 69.5; GPT-3.5 52.7 -> 42.8; GPT-4o 96.3 -> 96.7 (outlier, unaffected)
 setup: branch scenario, Table 3 ablation, six models
 quote: "When the tool name was removed, all models except the highly stable GPT-4o experienced a significant drop in accuracy (typically by 5%-15%)."
 where: 5.3.1, p.15, Table 3
4. Adding input/output parameter descriptions helps weaker models and is mixed for Qwen3.
 number: GPT-3.5 52.7 -> 61.1; Qwen2.5-7B 49.7 -> 60.6; Qwen2.5-14B 79.1 -> 84.2; GPT-4o 96.3 -> 97.5; Qwen3-8B 81.3 -> 81.3; Qwen3-14B 83.3 -> 81.5
 setup: as claim 3
 quote: "Interestingly, the Qwen3 series models appeared largely insensitive to this addition"
 where: 5.3.1, p.15, Table 3
5. Fine-tuning on data distilled from a routine-guided teacher internalizes the plan, so the student needs no routine at inference.
 number: Qwen3-14B No Routine 32.6 -> 90.2; with branch routine 95.5; without branch 98.0 (GPT-4o 96.3). All four small models reach 87.5-90.2 with no routine.
 setup: LoRA rank 8, 537 distilled scenario samples (3,108 labelled tool calls), epoch 3, 4x A10 24GB, lr 1e-4. Test set was also generated by GPT-4o with the same routines, in the same scenario.
 quote: "Qwen3-14B trained on this distilled dataset achieved an accuracy of 95.5% on the test set, approaching GPT-4o's 96.3%"
 where: Intro p.2; Table 2 p.14; 5.2.2
6. Fine-tuning on a generic routine-following set (4,209 BUTTON-derived samples) improves routine-following but hurts autonomous planning.
 number: Qwen3-14B with branch routine 83.3 -> 88.2; No Routine 32.6 -> 33.2 (Qwen3-8B 35.3 -> 23.4; Qwen2.5-14B 19.4 -> 30.9; Qwen2.5-7B 14.9 -> 22.4, so the no-routine direction is mixed in Table 2)
 setup: BUTTON 8,000 instances filtered to 4,209 (at most 8 steps, no nested structures)
 quote: "under the No Routine condition that requires autonomous planning, the performance of these fine-tuned models declined, indicating a trade-off"
 where: 5.2.2, p.14; Table 2. The prose says "declined", but Table 2 shows rises for three of four models and a fall only for Qwen3-8B. Treat the prose with caution.
7. A rough user draft already beats no plan. AI-refinement closes most of the gap to a human-annotated routine, but humans stay best for strong models.
 number: GPT-4o draft 71.2 / AI-optimized 90.9 / human 96.3; Qwen3-14B 70.9 / 76.7 / 83.3; Qwen2.5-14B 61.7 / 82.3 / 79.1 (AI beats human); Qwen2.5-7B 46.6 / 50.4 / 49.7
 setup: Table 4, GPT-4o does the optimization, branch scenario
 quote: "Even a low-quality user draft improved model execution accuracy."
 where: 5.3.2, p.16, Table 4
8. Distractor routines hurt. One correct routine is best, and adding unrelated ones lowers accuracy non-monotonically.
 number: GPT-4o 96.3 (1) -> 76.6 (2) -> 80.1 (3) -> 88.6 (5); Qwen2.5-14B 79.1 -> 55.8 -> 60.7 -> 71.3. Qwen2.5-7B (45.1/45.0/54.4) and GPT-3.5 (53.6/54.7/60.0) do not drop monotonically; GPT-3.5 even rises above its 52.7 baseline.
 setup: 2, 3 or 5 routines supplied, one applicable, order shuffled. The recovery explanation is a stated hypothesis, not tested.
 quote: "providing a single correct Routine is most effective for high-performing models. Their accuracy dropped significantly when even one distractor was introduced."
 where: 5.3.3, pp.16-17, Table 5
9. Branching in the plan costs weaker models accuracy.
 number: GPT-4-Turbo 99.0 (branch) vs 98.3 (no branch); Qwen3-8B 81.3 vs 81.3; Qwen2.5-14B 79.1 vs 79.2. Largest gaps are in the trained models, e.g. Qwen3-8B Common 82.8 vs 89.3.
 quote: "performance was generally higher in the w/o Branch scenario. The performance difference was small for high-performing models."
 where: 5.2.1, p.14
10. Design claims (stated, not measured): a small instruct model can execute while a larger one plans, and variable memory (store long tool outputs under a key such as memory_xxx so the model passes keys instead of values) cuts context, tokens and syntax errors. There is no ablation of variable memory and no measured cost or latency.
 quote: "The Variable Memory mechanism significantly reduces context pressure, and it also reduces token consumption and improves syntactic accuracy."
 where: 3.4.2, p.8

BASELINES (matched?): "No Routine" gives the model the user query plus the tool list and has it plan and call in one pass, with no ReAct loop and no model-written plan. The routine arms use the same models, the same 1,148 samples and the same shuffled tool order, so those arms are matched with each other. The routine arms get a human-written or GPT-4o-refined plan, which is extra information from domain experts, so this tests "plan quality" more than "plan vs no plan". Test samples are teacher-forced: each includes the true prior steps (history up to the current step), so errors do not compound, and accuracy is per step rather than per task. The test set was generated by GPT-4o using these routines, which favours GPT-4o and routine-following. The "Common" and "Scenario" fine-tunes cannot be compared with each other fairly, because the Scenario data comes from the test distribution (the same HR templates). Compared with each other, all models used Qwen3 reasoning off for the fine-tunes. No cost comparison of any kind.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: routines depend on expert drafts, so generalization is weak when tools or workflows change. They propose RL and a multi-agent routine framework as future work (Sec. 6).
- Not shown: end-to-end task success, latency, token cost, error recovery, or results outside one HR scenario with a Chinese-language prompt. No seeds or confidence intervals. Free-text parameters are scored by approximate matching (existence and type only, not content), which flatters parameter accuracy. The Table 4 "Human Annotation" column equals the Table 3 baseline. The 5-15 point tool-name drop is for most models and not for GPT-4o.
- Dated: models are 2025-era (GPT-3.5/4/4o, Claude 3.7, Qwen2.5/3). Preprint, not peer reviewed.

BUILDS ON: OpenAI Cookbook "Orchestrating Agents: Routines and Handoffs" (ref [15], origin of Routine); BUTTON dataset (PKU-Baichuan-MLSystemLab) for training data; BFCL (Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard) AST evaluation [59]; Wang et al. 2024 agent survey [2] (planning, execution, tools, memory); LoRA [56]; LLaMA-Factory/DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 [57,58]; MCP (Anthropic); Manus planner/executor/verifier [25]; AutoGPT, BabyAGI, AutoGen [18-20]; the authors' earlier single-step tool-calling pipeline [45]; knowledge distillation [55]. Reference numbers are as printed, and the citation list was not read in full.

CODE (verbatim, worth keeping)
1. Routine in natural language (App. B.1, p.24):
"Step 1. Get announcements: Download the latest employee handbook file from the company's internal system, use the fetch_latest_announcements tool;" (each step ends "use the <tool> tool;", and the last step with "and end the workflow;")
2. Branch notation (3.1.1, p.5): "Branch X-1 Step 1. <Step Name>: If <Condition>, perform <Step Description>, using the <Tool Name> tool;"
3. JSON routine schema (App. A.1, p.22): {"step": "1", "name": "xxxxx", "description": "xxxxxxxxxxxx", "tool": "tool_X", "type": "node"}; branch node types are "branch", "branchnode" and "finish", with step ids like "x-n_i" (i-th step of the n-th branch of main step x).
4. Executor system prompt skeleton (App. A.2, p.23): "Please strictly follow the routines, do not skip any steps, and only output one function call at a time." with <routines>{ROUTINES_DESCRIPTION}</routines>, <variables>{VARIABLES_MEMORY}</variables>, <tools>TOOLS</tools> and the variable-memory rule "When temporary variable memory_xxx appears in the result returned by the tool result... Try to fill in temporary variable memory_xxx instead of the actual value".
5. Routine-writer prompt (App. A.1): "Each workflow step must use a tool provided in the tool list, or perform branch condition judgment... Each step only uses one tool." Inputs {routine_draft} and {tool_list}.
6. Routine components (Table 1, p.5): step number, step name, step description, optional input description, optional output description, optional step tool (one tool per step).

FIGURE candidate: Figure 2 (p.4 to 5), "Framework of our Routine-based agent system". It shows expert-annotated planning prompt -> Routine generation -> small execution model -> MCP tools -> a dedicated summarization tool, with procedure and variable memory. It explains the planner/executor split faster than prose. Alternative: Figure 1 (p.2), the one-panel mechanism. Figure 7 (p.12) shows the structural -> tool selection -> parameter error hierarchy used for scoring. I did not run the figures script, so captions are taken from the text.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction is clean apart from some stray spacing. The prose and Table 2 disagree on common-FT no-routine effects (claim 6). Table 3 and Table 4 baselines do not use identical column labels. Conclusion's "approximately 50%" gain is 50.7 points. The Related Work attributes GraphFlow to AutoGen, which looks like an error. The paper says 5-6 query templates for each of 10 sub-scenarios, giving about 50-60 queries each, so the test set is template-derived and low in diversity. The HR test is Chinese-language.
